extracted.intended_audience: young-adult/general readers interested in privacy, hacking, and surveillance issues
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt (chapter) from a young-adult novel that explains and dramatizes surveillance, privacy engineering, and activist tactics while telling a story. The text mixes narrative with explicit technical/political observations about security systems and countermeasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security systems: evaluate by how they fail
rubrics_metrics.description: “The important thing about security systems isn't how they work, it's how they fail.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus evaluation on failure modes and brittleness rather than ideal operation. A system that seems effective in theory can be fragile in practice; broad automated screening can break when it catches too many innocents, causing systemic collapse or unacceptable harm. Test how the system behaves under stress, in edge cases, and when adversaries intentionally try to game it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox of the false positive
rubrics_metrics.description: When you try to find something very rare, even a test that is '99 percent accurate' will produce far more false positives than true positives; accuracy must be commensurate with base-rate rarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always compute base-rate effects: multiply test false-positive rate by population size to estimate how many innocents will be flagged. For rare-event detection (e.g., terrorism), ordinary detection accuracies (40–60% in practice) lead to huge numbers of innocent people being investigated. Design requirements must therefore demand very high precision (comparable to the rarity) or accept the social/operational cost of mass false positives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traffic-pattern profiling risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Encrypted traffic volume/ratios can be used to identify people. A normal user's session might be ~95% cleartext, 5% ciphertext; someone sending ~95% ciphertext stands out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating privacy or anonymity systems, include analysis of traffic-volume fingerprints and statistical anomalies. Designers must account for metadata and volume analysis as effective deanonymization vectors; defenders should avoid creating easily identifiable traffic profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization defense: change the baseline (increase population encryption)
rubrics_metrics.description: "What if the average San Francisco Internet user had a *lot* more crypto in his average day on the Internet? ... If we could change the split so it's more like fifty-fifty cleartext to ciphertext, then the users that supply the Xnet would just look like normal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A production strategy for privacy tools: to avoid singled-out encrypted users, raise the population baseline by encouraging common encrypted behaviors (e.g., routinely downloading large encrypted files). Product-design and deployment should consider social adoption and 'cover traffic' approaches (e.g., Pigspleen's indienet) so private communications blend into normal traffic distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational security (OPSEC): avoid public identifiers linked to private activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid saying or using handles in public once those handles are associated with sensitive activity: 'Don't use that name in public anymore.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy for activists/developers: treat online handles, organisational labels, and other identifiers as operational risks. When those identifiers become linked to clandestine or sensitive activities, public use can endanger people. Include rules in operational plans to separate public behaviour from sensitive handles and to minimize linkability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active anti-surveillance tactic: create statistical noise (RFID/FasTrak swapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use inexpensive 'arphid cloners' to read and write RFID tags (FasTrak/Fast Pass) and randomly swap people's tag codes so everyone's profiles skew and make bulk profiling ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical guidance for activism: creating widespread, randomized noise in surveillance data can overload profiling and produce systemic gridlock (Operation False Positive example). However, designers/organizers must consider legality, ethics, and collateral effects (economic disruption, people inconvenienced, potential danger). The text documents both the technique and its real-world effects (traffic/gridlock, longer lines, disrupted services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh collateral harm and proportionality of tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical reflection from characters: tactics that 'turn the whole city into terrorism suspects' or put people in danger are morally and strategically questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning or evaluating counter-surveillance actions, include criteria for assessing collateral damage, proportionality, and moral acceptability. Consider whether a tactic disproportionately harms innocents, disrupts essential services, or undermines public support; such considerations may counsel for alternative, less-destructive forms of protest or technical mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empowerment through programming: learn to build tools yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer 'does exactly what you tell it to do' — learning to program (e.g., Python) lets ordinary people design tools and take control of machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For producing privacy tools or security countermeasures, include as part of capacity-building the recommendation that practitioners learn programming fundamentals. Practical guidance: start with approachable languages (Python), understand that code is precise instruction, and use this literacy to audit, build, or adapt systems rather than rely solely on others.
